name: Weme Gbe
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only Kluge 2011 Gbe comparative/subclassification work cited; no Weme-specific phonology found.

new_statements.quote: In this paper I show that Wemɛgbe, a language spoken in southern Benin, has two underlying tones, H and L, and that the surface tones M, LH and HL are derived by phonological rules. [p. 65] ... Cette étude nous a permis de voir que, comme dans les autres langues gbe, le wemɛgbe oppose deux tons sous-jacents symbolisés par B et H. Les autres tons sont des tons dérivés de ces deux tons de base. [p. 85]
new_statements.translation: This study has allowed us to see that, as in the other Gbe languages, Wemɛgbe contrasts two underlying tones symbolised by L and H. The other tones are tones derived from these two basic tones.
new_statements.citation: Gbéto, Flavien (2004). Esquisse de la tonologie synchronique du wemɛgbe, dialecte gbe du sud-Bénin. Studies in African Linguistics 33(1): 65-90.
new_statements.locator: Abstract, p. 65 (English); §7 Conclusion, p. 85 (French); tonemic argument §6.1, pp. 77-78
new_statements.translation_language: English (abstract) and French (conclusion; diacritics restored from the OCR layer)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible primary description is a tonology: Weme Gbe is a two-tone language (underlying H vs L; surface M, LH, HL derived, partly conditioned by the voicing of the root-initial consonant). The paper makes no statement of any kind about word stress or accent, so no stress placement can be read from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the tonal analysis notes exceptions for coronal /t/ numerals (§6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonology of nominal and verbal roots in citation form (verbs cited in the imperative, the Gbe citation form). Dialect of Agonlin-Lowé and Akpadanou (commune of Adjohoun, Ouémé).
new_statements.identity_note: Gbéto 2004 describes the wemɛgbe of the villages Agonlin-Lowé and Akpadanou, commune of Adjohoun (Ouémé, Benin); Glottolog weme1239 lists no dialects, so this is the language-level entry. Houndekan 1983 treats the Adjohoun (Ajowun) chef-lieu variety. Names: Weme Gbe, Wémé, Wéménugbé, wemɛgbe, Wemenu.

sources.note: Nothing about stress/accent anywhere (full scanned text searched for accent, stress, intensité, proéminence, accentu-, emphase; 'accent' occurs only for the grave/acute diacritics). States that Wemɛgbe has two underlying tones H and L (B), with M, LH and HL derived (abstract p. 65; §6.1 p. 77-78; conclusion p. 85). Consonant classes condition tone realization; the dialect described is that of Agonlin-Lowé and Akpadanou, commune of Adjohoun.
